title: Grilled Tilapia
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Four medium tilapia marinated as little as five minutes, over charcoal burnt down half an hour — and Ghanaians feel cheated if you don't leave the head on.
longDesc: Grilled tilapia with banku is the Ghanaian plate most likely to be eaten outdoors, and the recipe is simple enough to be mostly about the fire. Two pounds of charcoal is lit and allowed to burn down for about half an hour. Four medium tilapia, about half a pound each, are marinated at least five to fifteen minutes in grated shallots, oil, salt, cayenne, about a quarter cup of fresh chilli and grated ginger. After three to five minutes the fish is turned, and it should cook in about ten to fifteen minutes. The tip that matters most is cultural: leave the head on.
ingredients: 1/2 tsp hot ground cayenne pepper, or to taste
About 1/4 cup (4 tbsp) fresh chilli pepper
About 1/2 tsp peeled, grated fresh ginger
steps: Light the charcoal — about 2 pounds — and allow it to burn down for about half an hour.
Clean and score the tilapia, leaving the heads on.
Mix the grated shallots, oil, salt, cayenne, fresh chilli and ginger.
Marinate the fish at least 5 to 15 minutes.
Lay the fish on the grill.
After 3 to 5 minutes, turn the fish over.
It should cook in about 10 to 15 minutes in total.
chefTips: Leave the head on. Barbara Baeta's line, as reported, is that Ghanaians feel cheated if you don't — and it is also the best-eating part of the fish.
Charcoal burnt down for half an hour means grey coals, not flames. Tilapia skin on open flame is a disaster.
Five to fifteen minutes is a very short marinade and it is deliberate — fresh tilapia does not want to be sat in salt and acid.
Turn once, after three to five minutes. Repeated turning tears the skin.
Ten to fifteen minutes total for a half-pound fish. No sensory cue is published, so go by the flesh at the thickest point near the bone.
A quarter cup of fresh chilli for four fish is generous. It is a wet marinade rather than a dry rub.
Score the fish before marinating so the mixture reaches the flesh — not in the source, but standard practice.
commonMistakes: Grilling over flames rather than burnt-down coals.
A long marinade, which makes the flesh mushy.
sources: Adapted from 'Great Grilling: Recipes #58 (Grilled Tilipia) and #59 (Grilled Prawns/Shrimp), and a plea to African entrepreneurs', betumiblog.blogspot.com, timestamped 2011-06-22. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 7:53 PM'. The title's misspelling 'Tilipia' is as printed. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS) except the yield.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 4 medium tilapia, with a printed weight of about ½ lb each — THE 4-FISH YIELD IS SINGLE-PASS; '2 Tablespoons grated shallots or onion'; '1 Tablespoon vegetable oil, like canola'; '~a teaspoon of salt'; '1/2 teaspoon hot ground cayenne pepper or to taste'; 'about 1/4 cup (4 Tablespoons) of fresh chili pepper'; '~ 1/2 teaspoon peeled, grated fresh ginger'.
THE FIRE, as printed: 'light the charcoal (about 2 pounds) and allow it to burn down for about half an hour'. That is an unusually specific instruction and it is the most useful thing on the page.
TIMES as printed: marinate 'at least 5 to 15 minutes'; 'After 3-5 minutes, turn over the fish'; 'it should cook in about 10 to 15 minutes'.
NO EXPLICIT DONENESS CUE is printed — only the time window. That absence is recorded, and the guidance about checking the flesh near the bone is labelled as editorial in the tips.

THE CULTURAL TIP, SINGLE-PASS and attributed on the page to Barbara Baeta: 'Ghanaians feel cheated if you don't leave the head on'. Baeta is the Accra chef and co-author whose teaching also lies behind GHA046, GHA067 and GHA088.
SCORING THE FISH is not in the source and is flagged in the tips as standard practice rather than instruction.

A SECOND DOCUMENTED GRILLED TILAPIA, published at GHA095, takes a very different approach — a one-hour-to-overnight marinade and twenty-five minutes on the grill against this version's fifteen minutes marinating and fifteen minutes cooking. Neither is corrected toward the other.
The companion prawn recipe from the same post is published at GHA096.
storage: 2 days refrigerated. Grilled fish is best eaten hot.
reheating: Briefly under a hot grill, or eat cold.
healthBenefits: Tilapia is lean, high in protein and low in mercury.
Grilled with only a tablespoon of oil for four fish.
Ginger and chilli both carry documented bioactive compounds.
culturalNote: Grilled tilapia with banku and a pot of shito, eaten at a plastic table with a cold drink, is as close to a Ghanaian national meal as anything. The insistence on leaving the head on is not sentiment — the cheeks and the collar are the best eating, and serving a headless fish reads as cheating someone.
